claims.text: Combining enhanced free-energy sampling with calibration from selective in-situ neutron imaging will accurately and efficiently determine melting and liquid-state thermodynamic properties across the high-entropy-alloy family.
The proposed approach can determine melting temperature, fusion enthalpy, fusion entropy, volume change at melting, and liquid-phase thermodynamic properties.
Equiatomic CoCrCu can be changed toward equiatomic CoCrCuNi by adding Ni.
High-temperature neutron imaging can observe melting, solidification, and liquid-state phase behavior in CoCrCu-based alloys during heating and cooling.
Near the melting transition, solid and liquid phases may coexist or transition rapidly under controlled heating and cooling.
Enhanced free-energy calculations can construct a detailed landscape that captures subtle free-energy differences among multiphase states and complex liquid interactions in HEAs.
Advanced sampling techniques effectively navigate the high-dimensional, complex free-energy surfaces of multicomponent alloys.
In-situ neutron imaging can provide observations of liquid miscibility, phase separation, and phase transitions for calibration.
Coupling enhanced simulations to neutron-imaging data ensures accurate calibration of liquid-phase behavior and phase transitions.
The integrated approach will predict melting temperatures to approximately ±15 °C.
The integrated approach will predict fusion enthalpy and entropy within approximately 10% error.
The integrated approach will determine melting-associated volume changes in agreement with in-situ imaging across varied HEA compositions.
Conventional DSC, calorimetry, and basic CALPHAD models lack the resolution or efficiency needed for compositionally complex HEAs.
Neutron-imaging applicability depends on sufficient neutron-transmission contrast among the alloying elements or phases.
The method is restricted to systems for which sufficient computational resources are available for enhanced free-energy sampling.
Alloy-specific interactions and simulation-to-experiment calibration bias may cause performance to vary among HEAs.
A decisive validation can compare enhanced-sampling predictions against neutron imaging and DSC measurements over a series of HEAs under controlled thermal cycles.
The approach is invalidated if melting-temperature error exceeds ±15 °C, fusion enthalpy or entropy error exceeds 10%, or predicted liquid miscibility or phase separation conflicts with imaging.
